newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli economic policy scored at forum.
newsitem.headline: Israeli economic policy scored at forum.

text.p: Israel's economic and business leaders on Sunday sharply criticised the Bank of Israel's tough line on inflation and the government's failure to move quickly to implement structural reforms.
Business leaders also criticised the government's handling of the peace process.
"The government showed great courage in cutting expenditures but lost the grace period of its first year to make structural changes," said Shmuel Slavin, director-general of the Finance Ministry.
"We must focus efforts in this area in 1998 knowing that if we don't do it in the coming year it doesn't seem likely it will be done before the end of the current government," Slavin said.
He was speaking at a two-day annual conclave of Israel's business, political and economic leaders at the seaside resort town of Caesaria sponsored by the Israel Democracy Institute.
Benjamin Gaon, president and CEO of Koor Industries, Israel's biggest industrial holding company, said that the drift in government economic policy was discouraging foreign investment.

"We're facing a cloud of uncertainty in policy and strategy. We need a clear-cut strategy of where we are going," he told reporters. "The trigger is to reduce interest rates...but I agree that it is package deal."
Slavin said the Bank of Israel had also failed to respond adequately to the government's 1997 spending cuts.
Slavin, who took over the director-general's post in April, said the central bank's monetary policy did not react to the budgetary changes as it should have.
He said the central bank's monetary policy, which caused nominal interests to rise sharply last year, was excessive and had caused a needless slowdown.
After rapid growth most of this decade, Israel's gross domestic product grew a comparatively slow 4.4 percent in 1996 and at a 2.8 percent annualised pace in first-quarter 1997.

Slavin and others said that the central bank was incorrectly focused on controlling inflation and noted that its mandate was to consider other aspects of the economy as well in determining monetary policy. Slavin said he questioned the need for inflation targets, which the government has set this year at seven to 10 percent.
Yoram Gabbai, a former Treasury revenues director and now a fund manager, faulted the government for policy inaction in its first year in office.
"This leads me to conclude there will be zero growth in the next few years," he said.
"The peace process is stuck and is expected to influence for the worse the economic situation," said investment banker Aharon Dovrat.
"Foreign investors are looking at Israel today with a feeling of second thoughts," said Gaon. "It's not as it used to be. There is a general feeling that we need more action, not declarations."

He said that because of dismay with the direction of the economy and peace, Koor was seeking to diversify out of Israel. By the year 2000, he said, the company's goal is to have 50 percent of its projected $5 billion in revenues come from outside the country.
